evidence.quote:
Effect of Graded Sensorimotor Retraining on Pain Intensity
in Patients With Chronic Low Back Pain
A Randomized Clinical Trial
Matthew K. Bagg, PhD; Benedict M. Wand, PhD; Aidan G. Cashin, PhD; Hopin Lee, PhD; Markus Hübscher, PhD;
Tasha R. Stanton, PhD; Neil E. O'Connell, PhD; Edel T. O'Hagan, MSc; Rodrigo R. N. Rizzo, MSc; Michael A. Wewege, MSc;
Martin Rabey, PhD; Stephen Goodall, PhD; Sopany Saing, MPH; Serigne N. Lo, PhD; Hannu Luomajoki, PhD;
Robert D. Herbert, PhD; Chris G. Maher, DMedSc; G. Lorimer Moseley, PhD; James H. McAuley, PhD
IMPORTANCE The effects of altered neural processing, defined as altering neural networks
responsible for perceptions of pain and function, on chronic pain remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE To estimate the effect of a graded sensorimotor retraining intervention
(RESOLVE) on pain intensity in people with chronic low back pain.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This parallel, 2-group, randomized clinical trial recruited
participants with chronic (>3 months) nonspecific low back pain from primary care and
community settings. A total of 276 adults were randomized (in a 1:1 ratio) to the intervention
or sham procedure and attention control groups delivered by clinicians at a medical research
institute in Sydney, Australia. The first participant was randomized on December 10, 2015,
and the last was randomized on July 25, 2019. Follow-up was completed on February 3, 2020.
INTERVENTIONS Participants randomized to the intervention group (n = 138) were asked to
participate in 12 weekly clinical sessions and home training designed to educate them about
and assist them with movement and physical activity while experiencing lower back pain.
Participants randomized to the control group (n = 138) were asked to participate in 12 weekly
clinical sessions and home training that required similar time as the intervention but did not
focus on education, movement, and physical activity. The control group included sham laser
and shortwave diathermy applied to the back and sham noninvasive brain stimulation.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES The primary outcome was pain intensity at 18 weeks,
measured on an 11-point numerical rating scale (range, 0 [no pain] to 10 [worst pain
imaginable]) for which the between-group minimum clinically important difference
is 1.0 point.
RESULTS Among 276 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 46 [14.3] years; 138 [50%]
women), 261 (95%) completed follow-up at 18 weeks. The mean pain intensity was 5.6 at
baseline and 3.1 at 18 weeks in the intervention group and 5.8 at baseline and 4.0 at 18 weeks
in the control group, with an estimated between-group mean difference at 18 weeks
of -1.0 point ([95% CI, -1.5 to -0.4]; P = .001), favoring the intervention group.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In this randomized clinical trial conducted at a single center
among patients with chronic low back pain, graded sensorimotor retraining, compared with a
sham procedure and attention control, significantly improved pain intensity at 18 weeks. The
improvements in pain intensity were small, and further research is needed to understand the
generalizability of the findings.

8|IMPORTANCE The effects of altered neural processing, defined as altering neural networks
9|responsible for perceptions of pain and function, on chronic pain remains unclear.
10|OBJECTIVE To estimate the effect of a graded sensorimotor retraining intervention
11|(RESOLVE) on pain intensity in people with chronic low back pain.
12|DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This parallel, 2-group, randomized clinical trial recruited
13|participants with chronic (>3 months) nonspecific low back pain from primary care and
14|community settings. A total of 276 adults were randomized (in a 1:1 ratio) to the intervention
15|or sham procedure and attention control groups delivered by clinicians at a medical research
16|institute in Sydney, Australia. The first participant was randomized on December 10, 2015,
17|and the last was randomized on July 25, 2019. Follow-up was completed on February 3, 2020.
18|INTERVENTIONS Participants randomized to the intervention group (n = 138) were asked to
19|participate in 12 weekly clinical sessions and home training designed to educate them about
20|and assist them with movement and physical activity while experiencing lower back pain.
21|Participants randomized to the control group (n = 138) were asked to participate in 12 weekly
22|clinical sessions and home training that required similar time as the intervention but did not
23|focus on education, movement, and physical activity. The control group included sham laser
24|and shortwave diathermy applied to the back and sham noninvasive brain stimulation.
25|MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES The primary outcome was pain intensity at 18 weeks,
26|measured on an 11-point numerical rating scale (range, 0 [no pain] to 10 [worst pain
27|imaginable]) for which the between-group minimum clinically important difference
28|is 1.0 point.
29|RESULTS Among 276 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 46 [14.3] years; 138 [50%]
30|women), 261 (95%) completed follow-up at 18 weeks. The mean pain intensity was 5.6 at
31|baseline and 3.1 at 18 weeks in the intervention group and 5.8 at baseline and 4.0 at 18 weeks
32|in the control group, with an estimated between-group mean difference at 18 weeks
33|of -1.0 point ([95% CI, -1.5 to -0.4]; P = .001), favoring the intervention group.
34|CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In this randomized clinical trial conducted at a single center
35|among patients with chronic low back pain, graded sensorimotor retraining, compared with a
36|sham procedure and attention control, significantly improved pain intensity at 18 weeks. The
37|improvements in pain intensity were small, and further research is needed to understand the
38|generalizability of the findings.

44|back pain caused by a serious medical condition (ie, infec-

46|in the past 6 months, who had undergone spinal surgery in the

57|interventions contained treatments that targeted central ner-

59|ward functioning of the back. Participants were informed that
60|some of the treatments were not active. No further informa-

3|Abstract
4|Background: Statistical analysis plans describe the planned data management and analysis for clinical
5|trials. This supports transparent reporting and interpretation of clinical trial results. This paper reports the
6|statistical analysis plan for the RESOLVE clinical trial. The RESOLVE trial assigned participants with
7|chronic low back pain to graded sensory-motor precision training or sham-control.
8|Results: We report the planned data management and analysis for the primary and secondary outcomes.
9|The primary outcome is pain intensity at 18-weeks post randomisation. We will use mixed-effects models
10|to analyse the primary and secondary outcomes by intention-to-treat. We will report adverse effects in full.
11|We also describe analyses if there is non-adherence to the interventions, data management procedures and
12|our planned reporting of results.
13|Conclusion: This statistical analysis plan will minimise the potential for bias in the analysis and reporting
14|of results from the RESOLVE trial.

3|Introduction
4|Background and rationale
5|Low back pain is a burdensome and disabling health condition.1,2 People who experience low back pain for
6|longer than three months have a low chance of recovery and experience substantial functional and financial
7|difficulty.3210 Results of clinical trials of contemporary interventions indicate that, on average, people with
8|persistent low back pain experience small to no benefit, compared to control. Accordingly, there is an
9|urgent need to develop more effective interventions.
10|Recent progress in understanding the role of the central nervous system (CNS) in the low back pain
11|experience bears promise for the development of new treatment approaches. Accumulating data indicate
12|that people with persistent low back pain have differences in CNS structure, function, and biochemistry;
13|compared to people without pain.11220 Research has demonstrated that these differences may be related to
14|aspects of the low back pain experience.21223
15|Interventions designed to target the CNS (termed herein, psychophysical interventions) have been
16|developed and tested in a number of small studies.24227 Further research has combined these new
17|interventions with traditional interventions directed towards functioning of the back, or psychological
18|aspects of the pain experience. These data suggest that there may be additional benefit from a combined
19|approach.28232 Work is underway to evaluate these treatment programs in adequately powered,
20|prospectively registered, randomised controlled trials.33235
21|Aim
22|The aim of the RESOLVE Trial is to evaluate the effectiveness of a psychophysical-traditional intervention
23|(graded sensory-motor precision training) compared to a sham intervention for reducing pain intensity for
24|people with persistent low back pain at 18-weeks post-randomisation. This statistical analysis plan reports
25|the planned analyses of primary and secondary outcomes.
26|Study Methods
27|Trial design
28|The RESOLVE Trial is a two-group, parallel, randomised clinical trial with 1:1 allocation. Participants and
29|outcome assessors are blinded to group allocation and study hypotheses.33

12|The advantages of the intervention studied here include
13|that rates of adverse events were low. Other interventions for
14|low back pain, such as medications, surgery, and spinal cord
15|stimulation, have a greater number of adverse effects. For ex-
16|ample, opioids are associated with physical dependence, hy-
17|peralgesia, and life-threatening respiratory depression at high
18|doses.24 Other medicines recommended for low back pain, in-
19|cluding nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, have adverse
20|effects such as gastrointestinal or cardiovascular symptoms.
21|Guidelines for the management of low back pain caution
22|againstpharmacologicalinterventionforthesereasons.5Future
23|studies should compare the intervention studied here with
24|pharmacological treatments.
25|Limitations
26|Thisstudyhasseverallimitations.First,treatingclinicianswere
27|not masked to group randomization. Second, insufficient re-
28|sources were available to collect data at 26-week and at 52-
29|week follow-ups in all participants. Third, outcome mea-
30|sures were all self-reported. This may have exaggerated
31|differences between the intervention and control groups for
32|participantswhowereawareoftheirgroupassignment.Fourth,
33|the study was conducted at a single center, raising questions
34|about generalizability of results, including in different racial
35|and ethnic groups. Fifth, the analytic plan assumed that data
36|were missing at random, but it is possible that data were not
37|missing at random.
38|Conclusions
39|In this randomized clinical trial conducted at a single center
40|among patients with chronic low back pain, graded senso-
41|rimotor retraining, compared with a sham procedure and at-
42|tention control, significantly improved pain intensity at 18
43|weeks. The improvements in pain intensity were small, and
44|further research is needed to understand the generalizability
45|of the findings.

6|The data will be analysed by intention-to-treat by a statistician blinded to group allocation. We will analyse the effect
7|of the treatment intervention separately for each outcome using linear mixed models with random intercepts for
8|individuals to account for correlation of repeated measures. The model will include terms for important prognostic
9|factors measured prior to randomisation and specified a priori. We will obtain estimates of the effect of the intervention

answers.justification: The captured supplement dates the SAP draft to March 2, 2020, and describes the approved primary endpoint/analysis as pain intensity at 18 weeks using a mixed-effects model. The main report says follow-up was completed February 3, 2020, and reports the corresponding 18-week analysis. However, neither source establishes when unblinded outcome data became available to the investigators making analysis decisions. The chronology raises a concern that the SAP was drafted after outcome collection, but collection completion, data cutoff, or a draft date alone does not establish investigator access. Under the question's uncertainty rule, neither a definitive nor probable timing judgment is sufficiently grounded.
unknowns: When investigators first had access to unblinded outcome data; whether the March 2, 2020 SAP draft was finalized before such access.

These establish SAP drafting after follow-up completion and the reported analysis, but not investigator access timing; no captured source passage resolves that missing event.

answers.justification: The SAP identifies one primary pain measurement: average pain intensity in the previous week on a subject-rated 0-10 NRS at 18 weeks. The report provides pain results at the specified primary time point and also reports follow-up pain at 26 and 52 weeks. It separately identifies recovery and response thresholds as post hoc outcomes and reports both 30% and 50% response definitions. Thus the inspected material does not show an eligible pain measurement selected from multiple eligible scales/definitions with only a favorable subset reported; the stated primary measure and the presented additional pain follow-ups/threshold results are reported.

For the approved 18-week mean difference, the SAP specifies a mixed-effects model with group-by-time terms and an 18-week contrast; the main report describes linear mixed models, estimates the between-group difference at 18 weeks, and reports that result. The report also discloses a separately specified complier causal-effect analysis and reports its estimate. The captured passages do not identify a set of eligible alternative analyses from which the 18-week primary estimate was selected based on results, nor a result-driven reporting choice. Although the SAP's chronology relative to unblinded access remains unknown, that uncertainty alone is not evidence of selection among analyses.
unknowns: Whether other eligible analyses were conducted but not reported, beyond the primary mixed-effects analysis and the reported complier causal-effect analysis.
